claim: Transporters from bacteria to humans contain inverted repeat domains thought to arise evolutionarily from the fusion of smaller membrane protein genes.
source: Transporters from bacteria to humans contain inverted repeat domains thought to arise evolutionarily from the fusion of smaller membrane protein genes.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary origin of inverted repeat domains in transporters, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: The small multidrug resistance (SMR) family provides an ideal system to explore the role of mutations in altering conformational preference since transporters from this family consist of antiparallel dimers that resemble the inverted repeats present in larger transporters.
source: The small multidrug resistance (SMR) family provides an ideal system to explore the role of mutations in altering conformational preference since transporters from this family consist of antiparallel dimers that resemble the inverted repeats present in larger transporters.
evidence: This claim is based on the structural similarity between SMR dimers and inverted repeats in larger transporters, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: A single conservative mutation introduced into an SMR dimer is sufficient to change the resting conformation and function in bacteria.
source: Here, we show using NMR spectroscopy how a single conservative mutation introduced into an SMR dimer is sufficient to change the resting conformation and function in bacteria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by NMR spectroscopy data and functional assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Conservative mutations can influence structure and function of transporters.
source: These results underscore the dynamic energy landscape for transporters and demonstrate how conservative mutations can influence structure and function.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Membrane transport proteins catalyze the movement of ions and molecules across the membrane by binding substrates on one side of the bilayer and undergoing conformational changes.
source: Membrane transport proteins catalyze the movement of ions and molecules across the membrane by binding substrates on one side of the bilayer and undergoing conformational changes (Jardetzky, 1966; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The alternating access model proposes that a transporter samples at least two different conformations that expose the substrate to the inside and outside environment of the cell membrane.
source: Structural and functional experiments have shown support for the alternating access model in which a transporter samples at least two different conformations that expose the substrate to the inside and outside environment of the cell membrane.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge from structural and functional experiments.

claim: The presence of inverted structural repeats within a single polypeptide chain is widespread in membrane protein transporters.
source: The presence of inverted structural repeats within a single polypeptide chain is widespread in membrane protein transporters (Shimizu et al., 2004; Forrest and biology, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inverted structural repeats have been proposed as a mechanism to enable alternating access exchange.
source: The presence of inverted structural repeats within a single polypeptide chain is widespread in membrane protein transporters (Shimizu et al., 2004; Forrest and biology, 2013) and has been proposed as a mechanism to enable alternating access exchange (Forrest et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Proteins with structural repeats are thought to arise evolutionarily from the fusion of smaller membrane protein genes.
source: Proteins with structural repeats are thought to arise evolutionarily from the fusion of smaller membrane protein genes, such as three or four transmembrane (TM) domain transporters that associate into oligomers to achieve the functional state (Xu et al., 2014; Bay and Turner, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The small multidrug resistance (SMR) family is found in bacteria and archaea.
source: One class of these proteins is the small multidrug resistance (SMR) family (Schuldiner, 2014; Schuldiner, 2009; Paulsen et al., 1996) found in bacteria and archaea
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SMR family proteins contain four TM domains and assemble into antiparallel homodimers or heterodimers which resemble the inverted repeat structure in larger transporters.
source: One class of these proteins is the small multidrug resistance (SMR) family (Schuldiner, 2014; Schuldiner, 2009; Paulsen et al., 1996) found in bacteria and archaea that contain four TM domains and assemble into antiparallel homodimers or heterodimers which resemble the inverted repeat structure in larger transporters.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge about SMR family structure.

claim: Homodimer transporters such as EmrE are able to insert into two opposing directions in the membrane (dual topology).
source: Homodimer transporters such as the multidrug efflux pump EmrE are able to insert into two opposing directions in the membrane (i.e. dual topology)
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EmrE topology.

claim: Heterodimers in the SMR family are comprised of two genes that each insert into the membrane in a single orientation (single topology).
source: whereas heterodimers are comprised of two genes that each insert into the membrane in a single orientation (i.e. single topology).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SMR heterodimers.

claim: The paired SMR (pSMR) subfamily is thought to arise from gene duplication and evolution of dual topology SMR genes.
source: The latter form the paired SMR (pSMR) subfamily and are thought to arise from gene duplication and evolution of dual topology SMR genes (Bay and Turner, 2009; Rapp et al., 2007; Rapp et al., 2006; Kolbusz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The similarity of the quaternary structure displayed by the SMR family with the pseudo two-fold symmetry seen in larger transporters suggests a role for gene duplication and fusion of smaller genes to give rise to transporters commonly found in higher level organisms.
source: The similarity of the quaternary structure displayed by the SMR family with the pseudo two-fold symmetry seen in larger transporters suggests a role for gene duplication and fusion of smaller genes to give rise to transporters commonly found in higher level organisms (Yan, 2013; Lolkema et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations and inference from structural similarities.

claim: Asymmetry between functional subunits may have a fitness advantage, such as for evolving substrate specificity and direction of transport.
source: The widespread prevalence of inverted repeats and divergent evolution from homo-oligomeric proteins suggests that asymmetry between functional subunits may have a fitness advantage, such as for evolving substrate specificity and direction of transport.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on evolutionary considerations.

claim: EmrE is a native E. coli transporter that couples drug efflux of cationic/aromatic compounds with the proton gradient.
source: EmrE is a native E. coli transporter that couples drug efflux of cationic/aromatic compounds with the proton gradient (Schuldiner, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The coupling stoichiometry of EmrE can proceed in a 1:1 or 2:1 proton:drug ratio.
source: It has recently been shown that the coupling stoichiometry can proceed in a 1:1 or 2:1 proton:drug ratio, where the protons are bound by the glutamic acid residues at position 14 in the dimer (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Protons in EmrE are bound by the glutamic acid residues at position 14 in the dimer.
source: It has recently been shown that the coupling stoichiometry can proceed in a 1:1 or 2:1 proton:drug ratio, where the protons are bound by the glutamic acid residues at position 14 in the dimer (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The relative energies between inward-open and outward-open states are identical for wild-type EmrE.
source: Since EmrE consists of an asymmetric and antiparallel homodimer, the relative energies between inward-open and outward-open states are identical for the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the symmetric nature of the homodimer.

claim: NMR spectroscopy reveals a separate set of signals in the spectrum for monomers A and B within the EmrE dimer.
source: NMR spectroscopy has been a sensitive technique to probe this asymmetry by revealing a separate set of signals in the spectrum for monomers A and B within the dimer (Cho et al., 2014; Gayen et al., 2013; Morrison et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous NMR studies.

claim: Conservative mutations located within or close to loop 2 of EmrE modulated the overall rate of conformational exchange between inward-open and outward-open states.
source: Previously, we discovered that conservative mutations located within or close to loop 2 of EmrE modulated the overall rate of conformational exchange between inward-open and outward-open states (Gayen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Loop 2 is comprised of approximately Tyr53, Ile54, and Pro55.
source: Loop 2 is comprised of a short stretch of residues (approximately Tyr53, Ile54, and Pro55) and adjoins TM2 and TM3 of EmrE (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural information shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Loop 2 of monomer A is located on the open side of the transporter and does not make intermolecular contacts with monomer B in the tetraphenylphosphonium bound form.
source: Loop 2 of monomer A is located on the open side of the transporter and does not make intermolecular contacts with monomer B in the tetraphenylphosphonium bound form, while loop 2 from monomer B is proximal to loop 3 of monomer A and near the bottom of the substrate cavity formed by TM1-3 (Figure 1A) (Chen et al., 2007; Vermaas et al., 2018; Ovchinnikov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and Figure 1A.

claim: Loop 2 from monomer B is proximal to loop 3 of monomer A and near the bottom of the substrate cavity formed by TM1-3.
source: Loop 2 of monomer A is located on the open side of the transporter and does not make intermolecular contacts with monomer B in the tetraphenylphosphonium bound form, while loop 2 from monomer B is proximal to loop 3 of monomer A and near the bottom of the substrate cavity formed by TM1-3 (Figure 1A) (Chen et al., 2007; Vermaas et al., 2018; Ovchinnikov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and Figure 1A.

claim: A heterodimer formed between wild-type and I54L mutant can induce a change in the conformational equilibrium between inward-open and outward-open states when bound to tetraphenylphosphonium.
source: Indeed, our preliminary experiments showed that a heterodimer formed between wild-type and a mutant from loop 2 (I54L) or a mutant from the N-terminal region of TM3 (I62L) could induce a change in the conformational equilibrium between inward-open and outward-open states when bound to the high affinity compound tetraphenylphosphonium (Gayen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A heterodimer formed between wild-type and I62L mutant can induce a change in the conformational equilibrium between inward-open and outward-open states when bound to tetraphenylphosphonium.
source: Indeed, our preliminary experiments showed that a heterodimer formed between wild-type and a mutant from loop 2 (I54L) or a mutant from the N-terminal region of TM3 (I62L) could induce a change in the conformational equilibrium between inward-open and outward-open states when bound to the high affinity compound tetraphenylphosphonium (Gayen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: PISEMA spectra of wild-type EmrE, L51I, and I62L displayed 10 peaks, confirming the presence of twice the number of peaks as tyrosine residues in the primary sequence of EmrE.
source: Each spectrum displayed 10 peaks, which confirms the presence of twice the number of peaks as tyrosine residues in the primary sequence of EmrE (Tyr4, Tyr6, Tyr40, Tyr53, Tyr60), and is consistent with previous observations (Gayen et al., 2013; Morrison et al., 2012; Gayen et al., 2016; Dutta et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by data from PISEMA spectra and citations to previous observations.

claim: Wild-type EmrE has a preference for monomer B in the heterodimer with L51I or I62L for the proton-bound form of EmrE.
source: These data indicate that wild-type EmrE has a preference for monomer B in the heterodimer while L51I or I62L prefers monomer A for the proton-bound form of EmrE (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: L51I or I62L prefers monomer A in the heterodimer for the proton-bound form of EmrE.
source: These data indicate that wild-type EmrE has a preference for monomer B in the heterodimer while L51I or I62L prefers monomer A for the proton-bound form of EmrE (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A minimal heterodimer comprised of a single conservative mutation can strongly influence the conformational equilibrium and perturb the energy landscape of EmrE.
source: Nevertheless, these observations demonstrate that a minimal heterodimer comprised of a single conservative mutation can strongly influence the conformational equilibrium and perturb the energy landscape of EmrE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NMR data presented.

claim: The skewed conformational equilibrium is preserved under sample conditions used to collect solution and solid-state NMR spectra.
source: Thus, under sample conditions used to collect solution and solid-state NMR spectra (i.e. isotropic and aligned bicelles, respectively), the skewed conformational equilibrium is preserved.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of solution and solid-state NMR data.

claim: The skewed conformational equilibrium is preserved under conditions in which Glu14 is deprotonated.
source: This result supports the conclusion that the skewed conformational equilibrium is preserved under conditions in which Glu14 is deprotonated.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data at pH 9.1.

claim: The equilibrium population of wild-type EmrE to assume monomer B in the heterodimer at pH 9.1 is approximately 96%.
source: Using the relative peak intensities of A and B signals in the spectrum, we estimated the equilibrium population of wild-type EmrE to assume monomer B in the heterodimer at ~96% (range of 90% to 99% based on standard deviation).
evidence: This is calculated from NMR peak intensities.

claim: The L51I mutation induces a free energy change of approximately 1.8 kcal/mol in the heterodimer at pH 9.1.
source: This value corresponds to a free energy of ~1.8 kcal/mol induced by the L51I mutation in the heterodimer.
evidence: This is calculated from the equilibrium population.

claim: Addition of ethidium induced significant spectral broadening and ablation of peak intensities in both wild-type and mixed dimer samples.
source: Addition of ethidium induced a significant amount of spectral broadening and ablation of peak intensities in both the wild-type sample and that of the mixed dimer where wild-type was isotopically enriched (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in NMR spectra shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Spectral broadening upon ethidium binding suggests intermediate chemical exchange, which likely stems from motion corresponding to exchange between inward-open and outward-open states.
source: These data suggest intermediate chemical exchange, which likely stems from motion corresponding to exchange between inward-open and outward-open states (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from NMR data supported by a citation.

claim: The conformational bias is reduced when the heterodimer is bound to ethidium.
source: From these data, it is likely that the equilibrium is less skewed in the mixed sample upon ethidium binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the spectral broadening observed.

claim: The effect of ethidium binding supports the presence of drug-induced dynamics in the heterodimer, which would enable conformational exchange needed for drug transport.
source: Furthermore, the line-broadening supports the presence of drug-induced dynamics in the heterodimer, which would enable conformational exchange needed for drug transport.
evidence: This is an inference from the NMR data.

claim: Tetraphenylphosphonium binds with greater affinity to EmrE than ethidium and significantly reduces the rate of conformation exchange.
source: Unlike ethidium, tetraphenylphosphonium binds with greater affinity to EmrE and significantly reduces the rate of conformation exchange (i.e. slow chemical exchange regime) (Cho et al., 2014; Morrison and Henzler-Wildman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The equilibrium population of wild-type to assume monomer B in the heterodimer with tetraphenylphosphonium bound is approximately 86%.
source: Using the relative peak intensities of A and B, we estimated the equilibrium population of wild-type to assume monomer B in the heterodimer at ~86% (standard deviation range of 79% to 92%), which corresponds to ~1.1 kcal/mol induced by the single mutant in the heterodimer.
evidence: This is calculated from NMR peak intensities.

claim: The L51I mutation induces a free energy change of approximately 1.1 kcal/mol in the heterodimer when bound to tetraphenylphosphonium.
source: Using the relative peak intensities of A and B, we estimated the equilibrium population of wild-type to assume monomer B in the heterodimer at ~86% (standard deviation range of 79% to 92%), which corresponds to ~1.1 kcal/mol induced by the single mutant in the heterodimer.
evidence: This is calculated from the equilibrium population.

claim: Drug binding would not trap the transporter into a single conformation in the transport cycle.
source: These data also provide evidence that drug binding would not trap the transporter into a single conformation in the transport cycle and is consistent with previous work proposing the substrate controls the rate of conformational exchange (Morrison and Henzler-Wildman, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data and supported by a citation.

claim: L51I and I62L displayed a strong phenotype toward ethidium and were indistinguishable relative to wild-type EmrE in growth inhibition assays.
source: From these data, L51I and I62L displayed a strong phenotype toward ethidium and were indistinguishable relative to wild-type EmrE.
evidence: This is observed in growth inhibition assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: L51I and I62L mutations appear to be fully functional and able to couple to the electrochemical potential to accomplish active drug efflux.
source: Thus, each mutation appears to be fully functional and able to couple to the electrochemical potential to accomplish active drug efflux.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth inhibition assay results.

claim: EmrEin and EmrEout expressed individually were unable to confer a phenotype to ethidium.
source: Resistance assays verified literature results (Rapp et al., 2007) that EmrEin and EmrEout expressed individually were unable to confer a phenotype to ethidium, whereas co-expression displayed a strong phenotype toward this compound (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in resistance assays shown in Figure 4B and supported by a citation.

claim: Co-expression of EmrEin and EmrEout displayed a strong phenotype toward ethidium.
source: Resistance assays verified literature results (Rapp et al., 2007) that EmrEin and EmrEout expressed individually were unable to confer a phenotype to ethidium, whereas co-expression displayed a strong phenotype toward this compound (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in resistance assays shown in Figure 4B and supported by a citation.

claim: Wild-type EmrE co-expressed with EmrEin or EmrEout revealed identical levels of conferred resistance relative to wild-type EmrE alone.
source: The experiments where wild-type EmrE was co-expressed with EmrEin or EmrEout revealed identical levels of conferred resistance relative to wild-type EmrE alone (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in resistance assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Wild-type co-expressed with E14Qin or E14Qout displayed growth inhibition.
source: Indeed, the results of these experiments displayed growth inhibition when wild-type was co-expressed with E14Qin or E14Qout (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in resistance assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The transporter complementation approach leads to heterodimer formation in the cell membrane.
source: Taken together with the robust phenotype of wild-type co-expressed with EmrEin or EmrEout, these results confirmed that the transporter complementation approach leads to heterodimer formation in the cell membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance assay results.

claim: When EmrEin was co-expressed with L51I or I62L, a significant reduction in ethidium resistance was observed on LB agar plates.
source: Remarkably, when EmrEin was co-expressed with L51I or I62L, we observed a significant reduction in ethidium resistance on LB agar plates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in resistance assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EmrEout co-expressed with L51I or I62L retained the same phenotype as the single-site mutant alone.
source: To the contrary, EmrEout co-expressed with L51I or I62L retained the same phenotype as the single-site mutant alone.
evidence: This is observed in resistance assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The L51I or I62L mutant expressed with EmrEin displayed a faster drop in optical density in liquid media resistance assays.
source: Similar to the LB agar plate results, we found that the L51I or I62L mutant expressed with EmrEin displayed a faster drop in the optical density, which signified a reduced ability to confer resistance relative to the same mutant expressed with EmrEout (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in liquid media resistance assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The fluorescence dropped approximately 3-fold faster for L51I co-expressed with EmrEout than L51I co-expressed with EmrEin immediately following the addition of glucose in ethidium efflux assays.
source: Immediately following the addition of glucose, the fluorescence dropped ~3 fold faster for L51I co-expressed with EmrEout than L51I co-expressed with EmrEin (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is observed in ethidium efflux assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The fluorescence value at steady state (3600 s) was significantly lower for L51I co-expressed with EmrEout compared to L51I co-expressed with EmrEin.
source: Furthermore, the fluorescence value at steady state (3600 s) was significantly lower for L51I co-expressed with EmrEout compared to L51I co-expressed with EmrEin (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is observed in ethidium efflux assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A change in the conformational equilibrium can influence the overall rate of drug efflux.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with the resistance assay results and support the conclusion that a change in the conformational equilibrium can influence the overall rate of drug efflux.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the efflux assay data.

claim: A previous study reported an ethidium efflux rate difference of 1.6-fold between wild-type E. coli and an AcrAB-TolC efflux pump knockout strain that led to a 30-fold difference in the minimum inhibitory concentration.
source: Note that a previous study reported an ethidium efflux rate difference of 1.6-fold between wild-type E. coli and an AcrAB-TolC efflux pump knockout strain that led to a 30-fold difference in the minimum inhibitory concentration (Paixão et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Modest transport rate differences can have deleterious effects on bacterial growth, which stems from increased ethidium accumulation that leads to irreversible binding to DNA.
source: This shows that somewhat modest transport rate differences can have deleterious effects on bacterial growth, which stems from increased ethidium accumulation that leads to irreversible binding to DNA (Jernaes and Steen, 1994; Lambert and Le Pecq, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mutant paired with EmrEout in a heterodimer would favor the inward-open/cytoplasmic-facing conformation.
source: Specifically, the mutant paired with EmrEout in a heterodimer would favor the inward-open/cytoplasmic-facing conformation (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data and topology information.

claim: The mutant paired with EmrEin will bias toward the outward-open/periplasmic-facing conformation.
source: Likewise, the mutant paired with EmrEin will bias toward the outward-open/periplasmic-facing conformation under the same conditions (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data and topology information.

claim: The conformational equilibrium favoring the outward-open/periplasmic state has a deleterious impact on the overall transport cycle.
source: Hence, the resistance assay results suggest that the conformational equilibrium favoring the outward-open/periplasmic state has a deleterious impact on the overall transport cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance assay results.

claim: A heterodimer with a conformation favoring the inward-open/cytoplasmic facing conformation gives no measurable reduction in phenotype.
source: In contrast, a heterodimer with a conformation favoring the inward-open/cytoplasmic facing conformation gives no measurable reduction in phenotype.
evidence: This is observed in the resistance assay results.

claim: The role of the pH gradient is to favor the inward-open conformation that is poised for drug binding.
source: This finding is in harmony with our prior observation that the role of the pH gradient is to favor the inward-open conformation that is poised for drug binding (Gayen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The primary kinetic steps in the transport cycle that influence the observed phenotype are the inward-open to outward-open and outward-open to inward-open rates for the drug-free heterodimer.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that the primary kinetic steps in the transport cycle that influence the observed phenotype are the inward-open to outward-open and outward-open to inward-open rates for the drug-free heterodimer (Figure 5G, see double asterisks).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: The populations were more skewed for the drug-free states than those for the drug bound states.
source: First, the populations were more skewed for the drug-free states than those for the drug bound states.
evidence: This is observed from the NMR data comparing different states.

claim: NMR experiments with ethidium indicate that the conformational exchange was not halted in the heterodimer.
source: Second, NMR experiments with ethidium indicate that the conformational exchange was not halted in the heterodimer.
evidence: This is observed from the NMR data with ethidium.

claim: The conformational bias does not result in a locked-state that would ultimately lead to loss-of-function.
source: The latter means that the conformational bias does not result in a locked-state that would ultimately lead to loss-of-function (i.e. no substrate turnover).
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR and functional data.

claim: Numerical simulations showed that the rate of drug transport was approximately 5.6-fold faster for a heterodimer of mutant and EmrEout versus a heterodimer of mutant and EmrEin.
source: Using these simulations, we found that the rate of drug transport was ~5.6 fold faster for a heterodimer of mutant and EmrEout versus a heterodimer of mutant and EmrEin (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulations using a kinetic model.

claim: Shifting conformational equilibria via specific rate constants in a transport cycle has a direct impact on functional output.
source: These calculations correlate with the enhanced phenotype and increased rate of ethidium efflux and provide evidence that shifting conformational equilibria via specific rate constants in a transport cycle has a direct impact on functional output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results and experimental data.

claim: A minimal heterodimer comprised of a single conservative mutation is sufficient to disrupt the preferred resting conformation.
source: Our observations demonstrate that a minimal heterodimer comprised of a single conservative mutation is sufficient to disrupt the preferred resting conformation and underscore the presence of a dynamic energy landscape where relatively small energy differences exist among conformations in the transport cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Relatively small energy differences exist among conformations in the transport cycle.
source: Our observations demonstrate that a minimal heterodimer comprised of a single conservative mutation is sufficient to disrupt the preferred resting conformation and underscore the presence of a dynamic energy landscape where relatively small energy differences exist among conformations in the transport cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the magnitude of free energy changes observed.

claim: There might be fitness advantages for having separate genes that form a hetero-oligomer or a single polypeptide chain where the structural repeats are contained within one protein.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, we hypothesize there might be fitness advantages for having separate genes that form a hetero-oligomer or a single polypeptide chain where the structural repeats are contained within one protein.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on evolutionary considerations.

claim: A single mutation can be introduced within the functional assembly of a hetero-oligomer that is not possible for a homo-oligomeric protein.
source: In these cases, a single mutation can be introduced within the functional assembly that is not possible for a homo-oligomeric protein.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the structural differences between hetero- and homo-oligomers.

claim: EmrE is able to carry out symport under certain conditions, including import of polyamines upon mutation.
source: In fact, in addition to EmrE's known antiport activity, it is also able to carry out symport under certain conditions (Robinson et al., 2017), including import of polyamines upon mutation (Brill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Conservative mutations displaying skewed conformational equilibria opens the possibility of modest evolutionary paths for achieving symport or antiport.
source: Therefore, the observation that conservative mutations can display skewed conformational equilibria and influence function opens the possibility of somewhat modest evolutionary paths for achieving symport or antiport.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: EmrE is expressed as a fusion construct with maltose-binding protein in the pMAL vector in E. coli BL21(DE3) cells.
source: EmrE is expressed as a fusion construct with maltose-binding protein in the pMAL vector (New England Biolabs Inc) in E. coli BL21(DE3) cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: For oriented sample NMR experiments, 15N-tyrosine labeled EmrE was expressed with IPTG for 4 hr at 25°C.
source: For oriented sample NMR experiments, 15N-tyrosine labeled EmrE was expressed with IPTG for 4 hr at 25°C in an amino acid mixture consisting of 19 amino acids at natural abundance (300 mg/L) and 15N-tyrosine (120 mg/L).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The heterodimer samples were prepared by mixing the two proteins (wild-type/L51I or wild-type/I62L) with a molar ratio 1/1.2, where the protein in excess was at natural abundance.
source: The heterodimer samples were prepared by mixing the two proteins (wild-type/L51I or wild-type/I62L) with a molar ratio 1/1.2, where the protein in excess was at natural abundance (i.e. NMR silent).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The two proteins used to prepare the heterodimer sample were incubated together at 37°C in the presence of 50 mM DTT for 1 hr immediately prior to reconstitution into lipids.
source: The two proteins used to prepare the heterodimer sample were incubated together at 37°C in the presence of 50 mM DTT for 1 hr immediately prior to reconstitution into lipids.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Oriented sample solid-state NMR experiments were acquired using an Agilent DD2 spectrometer at a 1H frequency of 600 MHz.
source: Oriented sample solid-state NMR experiments were acquired using an Agilent DD2 spectrometer at a 1H frequency of 600 MHz equipped with a 1H/15N double resonance probe manufactured by Revolution NMR (design of Peter Gor'kov; Gor'kov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Solution NMR experiments were acquired using a Bruker Avance III spectrometer at a 1H frequency of 600 MHz equipped with a TCI cryogenic probe.
source: Solution NMR experiments were acquired using a Bruker Avance III spectrometer at a 1H frequency of 600 MHz equipped with a TCI cryogenic probe.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: EmrEin consists of three mutations relative to wild-type EmrE (R29G, R82G, S107K) and induces the N- and C-termini to face the cytoplasm.
source: EmrEin consists of three mutations relative to wild-type EmrE (R29G, R82G, S107K) and induces the N- and C-termini to face the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a description of the construct design.

claim: EmrEout consists of three mutations from wild-type (T28R, L85R, R106A) and induces the N- and C-termini to face the periplasm.
source: EmrEout consists of three mutations from wild-type (T28R, L85R, R106A) and induces the N- and C-termini to face the periplasm.
evidence: This is a description of the construct design.

claim: EmrE requires two glutamic acid residues to confer drug resistance.
source: E14Q was selected since EmrE requires two glutamic acid residues to confer drug resistance (Rapp et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.
